c.tagline: The white-and-blue gateway to the Loire Valley's châteaux and vineyards.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed taxis are metered; Uber and Bolt also operate. Street-hailing away from ranks is limited, so booking by app or phone is the norm.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency line; 17 reaches police, 15 the ambulance (SAMU), and 18 the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Late-night bar crowds around Place Plumereau and petty theft near the train station warrant usual care.

hood_desc: The medieval old town around Place Plumereau, a square ringed by half-timbered houses that fills with cafe tables by day and students and bar-goers by night; the liveliest, most atmospheric quarter of Tours.
The eastern historic core around the Gothic Cathédrale Saint-Gatien, the Château de Tours, the Musée des Beaux-Arts and the Loire quays; the concentration of the city's landmarks and museums.
The area around the Gare de Tours and Avenue de Grammont, with the main shopping street, cinemas and transport links; a convenient, well-connected base for first-timers and Loire day-trippers.
The blocks around Les Halles de Tours, the covered market, packed with delis, wine merchants, bakeries and bistros; the foodie and market-shopping heart of the city.
The genteel Belle Époque district around the Jardin des Prébendes d'Oé and Boulevard Béranger, all leafy avenues and mansions; a calm, elegant residential base a short walk from the centre.
lodging: Best Western Plus Grand Hôtel Tours
Hôtel Mercure Tours Centre Gare et Congrès

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout France.

transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 5:00 AM to around 12:30 AM, with reduced frequencies on Sundays and late evenings.
transit.note: Tours' Fil Bleu network centres on a modern north-south tram line through the city, backed by an extensive bus network; the flat, compact centre is also very walkable and bike-friendly.
transit.pay: Buy tickets from tram-stop machines, on buses, or via the Fil Bleu app; a single ticket is about €1.70 and validates transfers. Rechargeable Fil Bleu cards give cheaper fares.

car.idp: Not required for EU licences; recommended for others

train: TER Centre-Val de Loire regional trains
TGV Paris-Tours (~1h, via Gare de Tours & St-Pierre-des-Corps)

transit.m: Fil Bleu bus/shuttle to city centre (~20 min)

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris); leaving small change or a euro or two for good service is appreciated but optional.

food.name: Rillettes de Tours
food.desc: Pork shoulder and ham slowly cooked until golden and shredded rather than pale and creamy - drier and darker than the Le Mans version, IGP since 2013.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: The covered market's charcutiers sell IGP rillettes by weight; taste before you choose a jar.

places.name: Charcuterie Hardouin
places.note: The best-known Touraine charcutier, widely stocked in Tours; a reference for rillettes and rillons.

places.name: Le Tourangeau
places.note: Small restaurant built on Touraine classics, a good place to eat rillettes as a starter with local wine.

food.name: Rillons de Tours
food.desc: Chunks of pork belly caramelised in their own fat until lacquered and dark - eaten cold as a starter or hot with potatoes.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Several stalls sell rillons alongside rillettes; the market is the city's food heart.

places.name: Charcuterie Hardouin
places.note: Traditional producer whose rillons are a Touraine benchmark and easy to find in town.

places.name: Le Tourangeau
places.note: Cooks the local charcuterie repertoire properly rather than as a tourist novelty.

food.name: Fouees
food.desc: Little bread-dough balls fired in a wood oven until they puff hollow, then split and filled with rillettes, goat cheese or white beans.

places.name: La Fouee Tourangelle
places.area: Rue de la Rotisserie, Vieux Tours
places.note: Wood-oven fouees served all-you-can-eat with a spread of Touraine fillings; book at weekends.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Buy the rillettes and Sainte-Maure that traditionally go inside a fouee.

places.name: Troglodyte fouee caves, Loire valley
places.note: Cave restaurants carved into the tuffeau cliffs upriver serve fouees straight from the oven.

food.name: Nougat de Tours
food.desc: Not a confection but a tart: pastry spread with apricot jam, filled with candied fruit and almond macaroon batter, glazed white on top.

places.name: Patisserie Sabat
places.note: Long-standing Tours patisserie; a dependable place to try the city's own tart.

places.name: La Chocolatiere
places.note: Historic Tours chocolatier and patissier, good for nougat de Tours and local sweets to take away.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Market bakers sell it by the slice, handy if you only want a taste.

food.name: Sainte-Maure de Touraine
food.desc: Ash-coated goat cheese log with a straw running through it, sold at every stage from fresh and lemony to dry and peppery.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Fromagers here will let you compare young and aged Sainte-Maure before buying.

places.name: La Souris Gourmande
places.note: Cheese-focused restaurant in the old town doing fondues, raclettes and Touraine cheese boards.

places.name: Le Tourangeau
places.note: Serves local goat cheese warm on toast or as a cheese course with Vouvray.

food.name: Beuchelle tourangelle
food.desc: An old-Tours dish of veal kidneys and sweetbreads with mushrooms in cream - rich, rare on menus, and a point of local pride.

places.name: Le Barju
places.note: One of the few kitchens still making beuchelle; modern cooking rooted in Touraine produce.

places.name: Le Tourangeau
places.note: Traditional Touraine menu; ask whether beuchelle is on that week.

places.name: Bistros of Place Plumereau
places.note: The half-timbered square and surrounding lanes hold most of the city's classic bistros.

food.name: Vouvray
food.desc: Chenin blanc from the chalk slopes just east of Tours, made dry, off-dry, sweet or sparkling - the region's defining white.

places.name: Cave de la Dive Bouteille
places.note: Wine bar and cellar in the old town pouring Loire growers by the glass.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Wine merchants inside the market stock the full Vouvray and Montlouis range.

places.name: Vouvray cellars
places.note: Tuffeau cave cellars a short drive or bus ride out of Tours offer tastings year-round.

food.name: Chinon and Bourgueil red
food.desc: Light, pencil-lead cabernet franc from just downriver - the Loire red that locals drink lightly chilled with rillons and goat cheese.

places.name: Cave de la Dive Bouteille
places.note: Small, knowledgeable list heavy on Loire cabernet franc, by the glass or bottle.

places.name: Bistros of Place Plumereau
places.note: Almost every bistro on and around the square pours Chinon and Bourgueil by the pichet.

places.name: Les Halles de Tours
places.note: Market wine stalls let you buy the same bottles to take back cheaper.

landmarks: Cathédrale Saint-Gatien
Flamboyant Gothic twin towers soar above dazzling 13th-century stained glass in this cathedral masterpiece, sheltering the touching Renaissance tomb of Charles VIII's children.
Place Plumereau
The photogenic heart of medieval Tours, where half-timbered facades lean over café terraces that buzz late into the night with students and visitors.
Basilique Saint-Martin
A neo-Byzantine basilica crowns the crypt tomb of Saint Martin, the Roman soldier-turned-bishop whose cloak-splitting charity made Tours medieval Europe's great pilgrimage stop.
Tour Charlemagne
This mighty surviving tower of the vast medieval basilica over Saint Martin's tomb looms above the old pilgrimage quarter, climbable for city views.
Musée des Beaux-Arts
In the former archbishop's palace beside a giant cedar of Lebanon, this refined museum treasures Mantegna panels, Rembrandt and elegant French salons.
Château de Tours
The riverside remains of the royal castle, with medieval towers intact, now stage acclaimed photography and contemporary art exhibitions above the Loire embankment.
Pont Wilson
The graceful 18th-century stone bridge of fifteen arches carries strollers over the broad, sandbanked Loire, offering classic views of the city's slate-roofed skyline.
Hôtel Goüin
A flamboyant Renaissance merchant's mansion whose sculpted facade miraculously survived wartime bombing, now hosting exhibitions in the heart of old Tours.
Jardin Botanique de Tours
The city's oldest public garden spreads medicinal beds, greenhouses, wallabies and centenarian trees, including a famed ginkgo, across a tranquil landscaped park.
Rue Colbert
A pedestrianized shopping street running west from the city center past the church of Saint-Julien and the Hôtel Goüin toward the old town around Place Plumereau.

train.note: No international trains. Tours has two stations: the central Tours terminus and Saint-Pierre-des-Corps on the high-speed line, 5 minutes away by shuttle - most TGVs use the latter, reaching Paris Montparnasse in about an hour and Bordeaux in 2. Regional TER trains serve the Loire châteaux at Amboise, Blois and Chenonceaux. SNCF advance fares open around six months ahead.

bus.note: Coaches stop near the station. FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus run to Paris, Nantes and Bordeaux, though the TGV is much faster. Rémi regional buses and organised château shuttles cover the Loire valley sites that the trains miss, such as Chambord and Villandry.

ferry.note: Tours is inland on the Loire, which is too shallow and shifting for scheduled navigation, so there are no ferries. Traditional flat-bottomed toue boats offer short river trips as an excursion.

half.name: Château de Villandry
half.blurb: A short drive west, this Renaissance château is world-famous for its geometric gardens, where ornamental vegetables and love-themed parterres form living embroidery.
